clinical_category: Acute hepatitis B - public health reporting
blueprint_topic: Communicable-disease reporting and jurisdiction-specific legal requirements
stem: A client is newly diagnosed with acute hepatitis B. Which nursing action is most appropriate regarding public-health reporting?

options.A: Follow the facility and state/local reporting process to ensure the case is reported to the appropriate health department, because acute hepatitis B is reportable in all jurisdictions even though the exact reporting workflow is jurisdiction-specific.
options.B: Send the client's complete medical record directly to CDC because individual nurses are universally required to notify CDC themselves.
options.C: Do not initiate any reporting process because only chronic hepatitis B, not acute hepatitis B, is nationally notifiable.
options.D: Treat reporting as optional unless the client specifically requests that the diagnosis be sent to public health authorities.

rationale: A is correct. CDC states that acute hepatitis B is reportable in all jurisdictions and that acute, chronic, and perinatal hepatitis B are nationally notifiable conditions. However, CDC also states that cases should be reported to health departments as specified by state, territorial, or local regulations and that rules governing whether health care providers, facilities, and laboratories report hepatitis B vary by jurisdiction. Therefore, the nurse should follow the applicable state/local law and facility process to ensure the case reaches the appropriate health department. B is incorrect because national notification to CDC occurs through public-health surveillance systems; there is no universal rule requiring an individual bedside nurse to send a complete record directly to CDC. C is incorrect because acute hepatitis B is nationally notifiable. D is incorrect because communicable-disease reporting is governed by law/regulation rather than being optional based on client preference. The final item preserves the national reportability of acute hepatitis B while avoiding the legally inaccurate assumption that every nurse in every state has the same direct reporting duty or workflow.
educational_objective: Recognize acute hepatitis B as a reportable/nationally notifiable condition and follow the applicable state or local reporting law and facility process rather than assuming a universal direct-to-CDC reporting workflow.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_document_title: Hepatitis B Surveillance Guidance; General Surveillance — Viral Hepatitis; How We Conduct Case Surveillance — National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System
source_version_date: Current CDC surveillance guidance accessed 2026-08-18; NNDSS case-surveillance page updated in 2026
source_locator: CDC 'Hepatitis B Surveillance Guidance' → 'Case Reporting / and National Notification': acute, chronic and perinatal hepatitis B should be reported to health departments as specified by state, territorial or local regulations; acute, chronic and perinatal hepatitis B are nationally notifiable. Same page → 'Case Ascertainment': rules requiring facilities/providers to report hepatitis B vary by jurisdiction. CDC 'General Surveillance' → Table 1-1 and Table 1-2: acute hepatitis B has national notification criteria and NNDSS event code 10100. CDC NNDSS 'How We Conduct Case Surveillance' → case reporting to appropriate health departments occurs according to state disease-reporting laws; case notification from health departments to CDC is a separate process.
source_claim_supported: CDC directly supports that acute hepatitis B is reportable in all jurisdictions and nationally notifiable, while specific provider/facility/laboratory reporting duties and workflows are determined by state, territorial, or local regulations and health-department processes.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Safe and Effective Care Environment → Management of Care, printed p. 7 (PDF p. 10): 'Report client conditions as required by law (e.g., abuse/neglect, communicable diseases)' and provide care within legal scope of practice.
correction_summary: Rebuilt the source item to correct a legal overgeneralization. The final version retains the CDC-supported fact that acute hepatitis B is reportable in all jurisdictions and nationally notifiable, but it explicitly distinguishes local/state case-reporting duties from national notification to CDC and directs the nurse to follow jurisdiction-specific law and facility process. This removes the unsupported implication that every bedside nurse has the same direct-to-CDC obligation.
audit_findings: The source item correctly treated acute hepatitis B as reportable but overgeneralized the direct reporting obligation and did not distinguish jurisdictional case reporting from national notification to CDC.
Fresh CDC review confirms acute hepatitis B is reportable in all jurisdictions and acute/chronic/perinatal hepatitis B are nationally notifiable.

CDC also explicitly states that provider/facility/laboratory reporting rules vary by jurisdiction and that cases are reported to health departments according to state, territorial or local regulations.
The final distractors exclude direct-to-CDC overreach, false chronic-only reporting, and optional client-consent-based reporting; none is defensible.
